title: Semiconductors and the p-n Junction

references.label: NCERT Physics Part II, Class 12 — Semiconductor Electronics

summary: Semiconductors conduct better than insulators but worse than conductors; doping them creates p-type or n-type material, and joining the two forms a p-n junction, the basic building block of diodes.
explanation: Pure (intrinsic) semiconductors like silicon have a small number of charge carriers, generated by thermal energy freeing a few electrons and leaving behind holes. Doping introduces impurities to deliberately increase conductivity: n-type doping (with a pentavalent element) adds extra free electrons as majority carriers, while p-type doping (with a trivalent element) creates extra holes as majority carriers. When p-type and n-type materials are joined, a p-n junction forms, with a depletion region at the interface that allows current to flow easily in one direction (forward bias) but blocks it in the other (reverse bias) — the basis of diode rectification.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking n-type material is negatively charged overall or p-type is positively charged overall — both are electrically neutral; the labels refer only to the majority charge carrier type.
Confusing intrinsic (pure) semiconductor conductivity with extrinsic (doped) semiconductor conductivity, which is far higher and far more controllable.
examples: A p-n junction diode allowing current to flow only when the p-side is connected to the higher potential (forward bias).
genZNote: Doping a semiconductor is basically recruiting extra 'carriers' on purpose — n-type brings extra electrons, p-type brings extra empty seats (holes) for them to fill.
